results.title: Option Elementary School Geo Zones 2023-2024
results.description:
2023 - 2024 Elementary option school 'geo-zone' boundaries for Seattle Public Schools.

Students who want to attend an option school need to apply. No one is assigned automatically to an option school. Each option school has a geographic priority area (geo zone). The geographic zone tiebreaker is for applicants to an option school who live within a defined area in proximity to the school. Please note that living within the geographic zone does not guarantee assignment to the requested option school, but gives a priority for admission after siblings. Geo Zones may change from year to year as a tool for capacity management.

results.name: School_Walking_Boundaries
results.title: School Walking Boundaries
results.description:
Seattle Public Schools (SPS) and SDOT work together to promote safe walking and biking to school, defining walk boundaries to determine transportation eligibility and providing maps and resources for families. 

SDOT's Safe Routes to School (SRTS) program offers maps showing safe routes, sidewalks, and safe crossing points, as well as the School Streets program to close streets to traffic for safer walking, biking, and rolling.

For most SPS students, Seattle Public Schools provides free transportation for students who live within their school attendance area but outside the school's walk zone. 

  • Elementary and K-8 schools have a 1-mile walk boundary. Eligible students are provided service primarily on yellow school buses.
  • Middle schools have a 2-mile walk boundary. Service is either by yellow school bus or ORCA card for the Metro.
  • High schools have a 2-mile walk boundary. Service is provided with an ORCA card.

 

Data represented is for the 2025-2026 school year.

This data provides two layers:
  • School Zones
  • School Walking Boundary
 
Refresh Cycle: Manually, Annually as required.
 
Contact: Safe Routes To School team

results.name: Seattle_Transportation_Plan_Pedestrian_Element
results.title: Seattle Transportation Plan Pedestrian Element
results.description:
The Pedestrian Element of the Seattle Transportation Plan (STP) is a blueprint to create a more walkable Seattle and provides a suite of pedestrian improvements across the City. The intent is to focus resources on access to public schools, parks, and light rail, streetcar, and frequent transit networks12, in areas where walking conditions are difficult, and where people most need to be able to walk.  It highlights the needs of people walking and rolling and guides future investments to achieve STP goals.

The process is based on an analysis of factors related to the STP’s goals of safety, equity, sustainability, mobility & economic vitality, livability, and maintenance & modernization. This data-driven prioritization framework helps the city provide targeted improvements that reflect community priorities, City policy objectives, and current data.  

Throughout the life of the STP, there will be opportunities to evaluate what has been implemented and what can be prioritized in future funding cycles, within the context of the STP's goals, funding availability and project readiness, and other emergent needs. Decisions made as we craft regular STP Implementation Plans will determine the pace of STP Pedestrian Priority Investment Network implementation.

results.title: Seattle Collisions Around School Zones  - Quade Rawlinson, Spring 2026
results.description:
This map of Seattle enables comparisons between higher collision areas, speed decreasing infrastructure, and proximity to schools which can be used to describe the general safety around school zones. Speed humps are added to represent infrastructure that decreases speed which may correlate with decreasing collision probability. Unlike as predicted, a school zone does not have more speed humps than surrounding areas of Seattle. 

 

The Speed Humps feature layer is added from an ArcGIS FeatureServer service from the Seattle GeoData portal. Tool: ‘Add Layer from URL’ (https://services2.arcgis.com/I9cUOJUZvdGAJncI/arcgis/rest/services/Speed_Humps/FeatureServer) The speed hump feature layer pop up includes an image of a random speed hump for context. 

 

The vehicle collisions feature layer was downloaded from the Seattle GeoData portal and added using ‘Add layer from file’ (https://data-seattlecitygis.opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/90a68d4709b54327a6bc1dfa1b900f8d_0/explore?location=47.614571%2C-122.333025%2C11). The collision layer contained a large amount of features, so I chose to represent the point data as a heat map. Areas that had more collisions in close proximity would have a higher ‘heat’ index. Clicking on any area within the collision layer will reveal the pop-up showing fatal and nonfatal collision statistics within the city of Seattle.

 

A pie chart representing the count of collisions by the street traffic control was created. 49% of the collisions that took place happened at sites where there was no traffic control.

 

The school zone feature layer was also downloaded from the Seattle GeoData portal and added using ‘Add layer from file’ (https://data-seattlecitygis.opendata.arcgis.com/search?q=school%20zone). The symbology used to represent the school zone layer is a simple black line. The pop-up for school zones is a general image depicting a designated school zone with official roadway signage. 

 

The school zone buffer was created by me using the ‘Use Proximity’ analysis tool. The purpose of creating a buffer around the school zones is to provide a visual representation of the amount of collisions that have occurred around these school zones. 

 

Two bookmarks were created, one showing the collision hotspot in the heart of Seattle, and the other showing an area of school zones with absolutely no speed humps.

results.title: Neighborhood Context - UHI and Tree Equity Score
results.description:
This map shows two neighborhood-level layers alongside Seattle public school locations.

The background polygons show the Urban Heat Island (UHI) intensity for each census block group — how many degrees Fahrenheit hotter that neighborhood runs compared to surrounding rural areas. Deeper red indicates more intense heat.

The Tree Equity Score layer (toggle on/off in the legend) shows how equitably tree canopy is distributed across neighborhoods, scored 0–100 by American Forests. The color breakpoints reflect meaningful thresholds in the scoring system:

  • Dark green (90–100) — at or above Seattle's citywide Tree Equity Score of 91. These neighborhoods meet or exceed the city average.
  • Light green (81–90) — above American Forests' minimum target score of 75, but below the city average.
  • Cream (75–81) — at or just above the minimum target. These neighborhoods are meeting the baseline standard but have limited buffer.
  • Orange (60–75) — below the minimum target. These neighborhoods have meaningful gaps in tree canopy relative to their population's need.
  • Red (55–60) — significantly below target. These neighborhoods have the greatest need for tree canopy investment.

School dots are colored by whether they fall in an extreme heat zone (8°F or more above rural temperatures) or a high heat zone (below 8°F).

Click any school dot or neighborhood polygon to see detailed data. Use the legend to toggle layers on and off.

results.title: Urban Heat Island Index
results.description:
This map shows the Urban Heat Island (UHI) intensity across Seattle's census block groups alongside public school locations.

The background polygons show how many degrees Fahrenheit hotter each neighborhood runs compared to surrounding rural areas, based on Climate Central's 2024 analysis. The color scale runs from cream (cooler) to dark purple (hottest), with a mean UHI intensity across Seattle of 8.3°F above rural temperatures:

  • Cream/light pink (below 7°F) — neighborhoods with relatively lower heat island intensity, one standard deviation below the city mean.
  • Pink to rose (7–8.3°F) — moderate to average heat island intensity. Most of Seattle's neighborhoods fall in this range.
  • Dark red to purple (8.3–13.5°F) — above average and extreme heat zones, one standard deviation or more above the city mean. Neighborhoods here experience the greatest compounding effect of hard surfaces, limited tree canopy, and elevated ambient temperatures. The darkest purple areas represent the most intense heat island zones in the city.

The 8°F threshold is significant — at this level, heat island intensity is associated with meaningful health risks, particularly for children, elderly residents, and those without access to cooling.

School dots are colored red if the school falls in an extreme heat zone (8°F or more above rural temperatures) and yellow if below that threshold. 71% of Seattle's public schools — 67 of 95 — fall in extreme heat zones.

Click any school dot or neighborhood polygon to see detailed data.

results.title: BSD School Locator Zone Lookup Instant App
results.description:
Accessible Map Description: Bellevue School District Attendance Areas

 

 

MAP SUMMARY

 

This map shows the Bellevue School District's attendance areas for the 2024-25 school year in the greater Seattle area of Washington State. The map displays a city-level view centered on Bellevue, covering parts of Seattle to the west, Kirkland and Redmond to the north, Sammamish to the east, and Renton to the south. The map illustrates overlapping elementary, middle, and high school attendance boundaries with school locations marked throughout the district.

 

KEY TRENDS AND PATTERNS

 

The Bellevue School District forms a compact, roughly square-shaped area in the center of the map, outlined by a thick teal border. Within this boundary, school attendance areas show a nested pattern where smaller elementary school zones fit within larger middle school zones, which in turn fit within high school boundaries. The district contains a high density of schools, with approximately 15-20 elementary schools (orange markers), 5-6 middle schools (blue markers), and 3-4 high schools (purple markers) clustered within the central district area. School boundaries often overlap, creating darker, multi-colored zones where different attendance areas intersect. The district appears densely served with schools relatively evenly distributed throughout, though with slightly higher concentration in the central and western portions near downtown Bellevue.

 

TABLE OF CONTENTS


 

  • Map Summary
  • Key Trends and Patterns
  • Geographic Context
  • Visible Features and Patterns
  • Legend Definitions
  • Additional Map Information
  • Data Notes
  • Visual representation: Shown as a thick teal outline with rounded corners
  • Distribution: Forms an irregular rectangular shape in the center of the map, encompassing downtown Bellevue and surrounding neighborhoods
  • Boundaries: The district extends from Lake Washington on the west (including parts of Mercer Island), north to portions of Kirkland, east toward Sammamish, and south to parts of Newcastle and Newport Heights
  • Size: Covers approximately 12-15 square miles of urban and suburban area
  • Visual representation: Large areas outlined in purple with semi-transparent fills, labeled with school names including "Sammamish HS," "Interlake HS," and others
  • Distribution: The district is divided into 3-4 large zones, each covering roughly one-third to one-quarter of the total district area
  • Pattern: High school boundaries extend across multiple neighborhoods and encompass several middle and elementary school zones within each area
  • Specific zones: Purple boundaries are most clearly visible in the northern, central, and southern portions of the district
  • Visual representation: Medium-sized areas outlined in blue with semi-transparent fills, labeled with school names including "Chinook MS," "Tillicum MS," "Tyee MS," and others
  • Distribution: Approximately 5-6 zones distributed throughout the district, each covering 2-4 square miles
  • Pattern: Middle school boundaries are smaller than high school zones but larger than elementary zones, creating a nested hierarchy
  • Overlap appearance: Where blue middle school boundaries overlap with purple high school boundaries, the areas appear darker with both colors visible
  • Notable locations: Chinook MS appears in the northern-central area, Tillicum MS in the central area, and Tyee MS in the southern portion
  • Visual representation: Small to medium areas outlined in orange/red with semi-transparent fills, labeled with school names including "Cherry Crest ES," "Ardmore ES," "Medina ES," "Bellevue HS," "Clyde Hill ES," "Enatai ES," "Sherwood Forest ES," and others
  • Distribution: Approximately 15-20 zones densely packed throughout the district
  • Density: Elementary zones are the smallest and most numerous, with multiple zones fitting within each middle school area
  • Pattern: Elementary boundaries create a patchwork pattern across the district, with higher density in the central and western areas
  • Overlap appearance: In areas where orange elementary boundaries overlap with blue middle school and purple high school boundaries, the combined colors create darker, multi-hued regions indicating multiple levels of attendance area coverage
  • Visual representation:
  • Distribution: School markers are distributed throughout the district boundary, with concentrations in the central and western portions
  • Pattern: Schools are generally evenly spaced within their respective attendance areas, typically positioned near residential centers
  • Approximate count: The map shows roughly 25-30 total school locations across all categories
  • Specific locations: School names visible include Cherry Crest ES, Ardmore ES, Medina ES, Chinook MS, Bellevue HS, Clyde Hill ES, Sherwood Forest ES, Sammamish HS, Interlake HS, Tillicum MS, Tyee MS, and numerous others labeled throughout the district
  • Visual effect: In most areas of the district, all three boundary types (orange elementary, blue middle, purple high school) overlap, creating darker regions with multiple visible outlines and semi-transparent color fills
  • Interpretation: These overlapping regions indicate areas where students attend a specific elementary, middle, and high school based on their home address - representing the complete K-12 pathway for that location
  • Heaviest overlap: The central portions of the district show the densest layering of boundaries, where multiple small elementary zones exist within larger middle and high school zones
  • Scale: 1:288,895 (city-level view)
  • Data timeframe: 2024-25 school year
  • Coordinate system: Standard web map projection (Web Mercator)
  • Data source: Bellevue School District School Locator public data and Washington Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) district boundary data
  • The map displays current attendance area assignments; families should verify their specific school assignments through the district's official enrollment process

 

 

COMPLIANCE METADATA

results.title: Neighborhood-Initiated Safety Partnership Program - Planned and Completed Projects
results.description:
The Neighborhood-Initiated Safety Partnership Program is a new effort funded by the 2024 Transportation Levy. From now through 2032, we’ll deliver safety projects across Seattle shaped by community input, with a focus on neighborhoods with the greatest needs. 

Current Projects

In 2026 and 2027, we are building projects in neighborhoods based on equity, safety, and where sidewalks are missing. 

To gather initial project ideas, we looked at what we’ve already heard from the community through the Seattle Transportation Plan, Home Zones, Safe Routes to School, and other outreach efforts. We also partnered with our Sidewalk Development Program and community organizations to host community walking tours and see existing issues first-hand. In each neighborhood, we selected the top community priorities that could be built within one to two years. These safety improvements will connect to new sidewalks, schools, parks, and bus stops. 

Stay tuned for updates as we gather future project ideas. We look forward to working with you to build safety improvements across Seattle.

results.title: Seattle Earthquake Medical and Aid Facility Accessibility
results.description: The Cascadia subduction zone (CSZ) is a high-tension meeting point of three minor tectonic plates (Juan de Fuca, Gorda, and Explorer) and the North American Plate situated 70-100 miles off the pacific shore. It passes through northern California, Oregon, Washington and parts of southern British Columbia. While there has not been a major earthquake (7.0 or higher) caused by the stress on the subduction zone in over 1,000 years, geologic evidence indicates that the CSZ is capable of producing large-magnitude megathrust earthquakes at the interface between the Juan de Fuca and North American plates (Goldfinger et al. 2012). Studies confirm that there is a 10%–14% chance that a magnitude 9 (M9) earthquake followed by a tsunami will occur along the Cascadia subduction zone within the next 50 years. (Marafi et al, 2020).

results.title: City of Seattle Affordable Units in Fully Affordable and Market-Rate Buildings
results.description: This map displays market-rate buildings with affordable units throughout the City of Seattle. Affordable units are rent and income restricted at various percentages of Area Median Income (AMI) and regulated by the Office of Housing (OH). Median income, imputed based on the HUD-published very low-income limit for a family of 4, is used to calculate the income limits. SMC Chapter 5.73 requires that rent limits not decrease nor increase more than four and one-half percent from the prior year. For purpose of calculating rent limits, OH uses the affordable housing industry's standard average household size assumption of 1.0 for 0-bedrooms and 1.5 per bedroom for larger units.

results.title: Collisions Around School Zones in Seattle, Washington
results.description:
Seattle is the most popular, populous, and visited city within the northern state of Washington. Though not the capitol of the state, Seattle is regarded as the economic and cultural hub of the state. Located on the eastern shore of Puget Sound, this city has over 140 miles of freshwater shoreline and over 50 miles of saltwater. A prominent feature from the city that is recognized around the US is Seattle's Space Needle tower. Seattle's iconic 184-meter Space Needle tower can be seen below in the first image.

Like any other major city, collisions are bound to occur. City dwellers are commuting to and from work and students are being dropped off at their schools in high traffic regions, which can increase the probability of accident occurrences. Collisions around designated school zones in Seattle are most of interest, as school zones have traffic laws in place to promote pedestrian safety around their campuses. As you drive through a school zone, there is typically a decreased speed limit, usually around 20 mph, that is enforced when kids are taken to school and back to their homes.

results.title: Understory_kelp_indicator_gdb
results.description:
OVERVIEW
This file geodatabase supports the Understory Kelp Abundance and Condition indicator under the Puget Sound Partnership's Beaches and Marine Vegetation Vital Sign (PSP Agreement 2026-50). It was co-developed by the Reef Check Foundation and Seattle Aquarium. It contains the survey data and reporting units used to summarize understory (subtidal, non-canopy) kelp abundance and trends at the site, sub-basin, and Puget Sound scales. It complements the Washington State Floating Kelp Indicator, which tracks canopy-forming kelp. The data will be updated annually as new survey years are added.

 

CONTENTS 

1. Reef Check Washington Subtidal Kelp Surveys, 2021–2025 (Understory Kelp Indicator) – point feature class 

This feature class contains 1,187 transect-level survey records collected by trained Reef Check Washington volunteer SCUBA divers at 57 sites across 10 marine sub-basins, from July 2021 through October 2025 (2021: 42 records; 2022: 180; 2023: 294; 2024: 342; 2025: 329). Records include counts of kelp and other algae, invertebrates, and fish, plus substrate, relief, and cover. Points show survey site locations, and all transects at a site share one coordinate. Each record has a sub_basin_code that links it to the sub-basin polygons.

2. Washington Marine Waters Sub-basins (Understory Kelp Indicator) – polygon feature class

This feature class contains 11 marine sub-basin polygons covering Puget Sound, Hood Canal, the San Juan Islands, the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and Washington's outer coast. They are the reporting units for the indicator. Reef Check survey sites are summarized within these polygons to report understory kelp status and trends at the sub-basin scale. The boundaries are derived from the Washington State Floating Kelp Indicator sub-basins (KelpForestsWA Floating Kelp Indicator Dataset; accessed October 2026), so understory and floating kelp can be compared across the same areas. The Southern Coast sub-basin currently contains no Reef Check survey sites.


SPATIAL REFERENCE

Both feature classes use NAD 1983 HARN StatePlane Washington South FIPS 4602 (US Feet), WKID 2927.

 

ADDITIONAL DOCUMENTATION
Detailed lineage, attribute definitions, and limitations are documented in each feature class's metadata. The data processing code is available at https://github.com/Seattle-Aquarium/understory_kelp_indicator.

results.title: Recreational Cannabis Zoning Review App
results.description:
This application is intended to help in identifying properties in the City of Seattle that lie within zones where major marijuana activity (MMA), as defined in Seattle Municipal Code 23.84A.025, may be allowed. The application identifies known existing cannabis businesses (MMA) and known uses such as child care centers, public parks, playgrounds, public schools, etc.  that may trigger a required setback or buffer for new cannabis businesses (MMA), all based on current information. The application is updated as frequently as possible when new information is received, but the City of Seattle cannot guarantee the accuracy of the information contained on this mapping application. By providing this application, the City of Seattle makes no claims, no representations, and no express or implied warranties, concerning the validity, accuracy, or reliability of this data. 

Each user of this application and each applicant is solely responsible for doing their own research and independently verifying that their desired major marijuana activity site meets all legal requirements including, but not limited to, dispersion and buffering requirements set out in Seattle Municipal Code 23.42.058, and any other requirements under State or Federal Law. The City of Seattle shall have no liability for any decisions made, or action taken, in reliance on this data. 

Locations marked as compliant and non-complaint are not officially reviewed by the City of Seattle until an application from the Washington State Liquor Control Board is provided to the City.    

Buffering and dispersion requirements must also still be met.

Sensitive Uses
• 1000 feet from Schools, Playgrounds - (Retail, Producers, or Processors)

• 500 feet from Public Parks, Child Care Centers, Game Arcades, Libraries, Public Transit Centers, Recreation Centers/Facilities (Retail)

• 250 feet from Public Parks, Child Care Centers, Game Arcades, Libraries, Public Transit Centers, Recreation Centers/Facilities (Retail within DMR or DMC zones in Downtown Urban Center, Producers, or Processors)

Dispersion 
• Only two retail stores are allowed to be located within 1000ft of each other.

results.title: BSD_School_Locator_Web_Map
results.description:
Accessible Map Description: Bellevue School District Attendance Areas

 

 

MAP SUMMARY

 

This map shows the Bellevue School District's attendance areas for the 2024-25 school year in the greater Seattle area of Washington State. The map displays a city-level view centered on Bellevue, covering parts of Seattle to the west, Kirkland and Redmond to the north, Sammamish to the east, and Renton to the south. The map illustrates overlapping elementary, middle, and high school attendance boundaries with school locations marked throughout the district.

 

KEY TRENDS AND PATTERNS

 

The Bellevue School District forms a compact, roughly square-shaped area in the center of the map, outlined by a thick teal border. Within this boundary, school attendance areas show a nested pattern where smaller elementary school zones fit within larger middle school zones, which in turn fit within high school boundaries. The district contains a high density of schools, with approximately 15-20 elementary schools (orange markers), 5-6 middle schools (blue markers), and 3-4 high schools (purple markers) clustered within the central district area. School boundaries often overlap, creating darker, multi-colored zones where different attendance areas intersect. The district appears densely served with schools relatively evenly distributed throughout, though with slightly higher concentration in the central and western portions near downtown Bellevue.

 

TABLE OF CONTENTS


 

  • Map Summary
  • Key Trends and Patterns
  • Geographic Context
  • Visible Features and Patterns
  • Legend Definitions
  • Additional Map Information
  • Data Notes
  • Visual representation: Shown as a thick teal outline with rounded corners
  • Distribution: Forms an irregular rectangular shape in the center of the map, encompassing downtown Bellevue and surrounding neighborhoods
  • Boundaries: The district extends from Lake Washington on the west (including parts of Mercer Island), north to portions of Kirkland, east toward Sammamish, and south to parts of Newcastle and Newport Heights
  • Size: Covers approximately 12-15 square miles of urban and suburban area
  • Visual representation: Large areas outlined in purple with semi-transparent fills, labeled with school names including "Sammamish HS," "Interlake HS," and others
  • Distribution: The district is divided into 3-4 large zones, each covering roughly one-third to one-quarter of the total district area
  • Pattern: High school boundaries extend across multiple neighborhoods and encompass several middle and elementary school zones within each area
  • Specific zones: Purple boundaries are most clearly visible in the northern, central, and southern portions of the district
  • Visual representation: Medium-sized areas outlined in blue with semi-transparent fills, labeled with school names including "Chinook MS," "Tillicum MS," "Tyee MS," and others
  • Distribution: Approximately 5-6 zones distributed throughout the district, each covering 2-4 square miles
  • Pattern: Middle school boundaries are smaller than high school zones but larger than elementary zones, creating a nested hierarchy
  • Overlap appearance: Where blue middle school boundaries overlap with purple high school boundaries, the areas appear darker with both colors visible
  • Notable locations: Chinook MS appears in the northern-central area, Tillicum MS in the central area, and Tyee MS in the southern portion
  • Visual representation: Small to medium areas outlined in orange/red with semi-transparent fills, labeled with school names including "Cherry Crest ES," "Ardmore ES," "Medina ES," "Bellevue HS," "Clyde Hill ES," "Enatai ES," "Sherwood Forest ES," and others
  • Distribution: Approximately 15-20 zones densely packed throughout the district
  • Density: Elementary zones are the smallest and most numerous, with multiple zones fitting within each middle school area
  • Pattern: Elementary boundaries create a patchwork pattern across the district, with higher density in the central and western areas
  • Overlap appearance: In areas where orange elementary boundaries overlap with blue middle school and purple high school boundaries, the combined colors create darker, multi-hued regions indicating multiple levels of attendance area coverage
  • Visual representation:
  • Distribution: School markers are distributed throughout the district boundary, with concentrations in the central and western portions
  • Pattern: Schools are generally evenly spaced within their respective attendance areas, typically positioned near residential centers
  • Approximate count: The map shows roughly 25-30 total school locations across all categories
  • Specific locations: School names visible include Cherry Crest ES, Ardmore ES, Medina ES, Chinook MS, Bellevue HS, Clyde Hill ES, Sherwood Forest ES, Sammamish HS, Interlake HS, Tillicum MS, Tyee MS, and numerous others labeled throughout the district
  • Visual effect: In most areas of the district, all three boundary types (orange elementary, blue middle, purple high school) overlap, creating darker regions with multiple visible outlines and semi-transparent color fills
  • Interpretation: These overlapping regions indicate areas where students attend a specific elementary, middle, and high school based on their home address - representing the complete K-12 pathway for that location
  • Heaviest overlap: The central portions of the district show the densest layering of boundaries, where multiple small elementary zones exist within larger middle and high school zones
  • Scale: 1:288,895 (city-level view)

results.title: Which School Zones Are Most Environmentally Vulnerable?
results.description:
Seattle, WA, is a fast-growing city with 14.6% growth in population between 2010 and 2020, largely contributed to by the growth of internet unicorns like Microsoft and Amazon (Trumm, 2024). The rapid expansion brought stress to urban development. As citizens settle down, now is a great time to take a look at the environmental risks within the city: Will roads be submerged? Will air quality affect people's lives?

Specifically, this research targeted 169 K-12 school zones within the 7 administrative districts in the city, taking a look at the most susceptible school zones in terms of air quality and water discharge. This study would be useful to city planners and policymakers to start considering potential prevention mechanisms towards the most susceptible school zones while learning from the best. It would also be a great material for parents of school-age kids -- this could help you in choosing the right school.

results.title: Fjord Estuaries: Washington's Hydrological Gem
results.description:
Fjord Estuaries: Washington's Hydrological Gem -- an environmental investigation by Druhin Bhowal and Siddhant Porwal, Tesla STEM High School.

The Puget Sound – the majestic and vibrant heart of the Pacific Northwest. Through its sparkling waters sail countless vessels, nourishing the dazzling, modern cities on its shores. At the same time, it shelters a rich and diverse array of ancient plants and animals in its fractalesque fjord estuary systems, creating one of the most splendid and unique ecosystems in the world.

The saga of the venerable Sound is as astounding as its manifold roles today. Our ArcGIS Competition entry delves into its remarkable history, revealing its glacial origins and the dramatic climatic changes that shaped its formation. Using vivid maps, imagery, and engaging language, we guide the viewer through 10,000 years of fascinating geology and ecology, ending with an examination of the Sound’s network of fjord estuaries and their astonishing biodiversity.

Yet this project is not merely a celebration of the Sound’s beauty and wonder – it is also a call to action to protect it from the ecological threats it faces every day. Distilling information from local, state, and national government agencies, we deliver a comprehensive evaluation of the anthropogenic factors most heavily contributing to the decline of the Sound. In addition, we offer a fresh perspective on modern conservation efforts and policy changes that must be made in order to keep the Puget Sound and its bountiful Fjord Estuaries secure today and forevermore.

We thank the NOAA, USGS, and UW Ecological Institute for their generous contributions to the realization of this project, both in terms of critical information and geospatial data. We also acknowledge the following sources:

  1. Dept. Natural Resources - Cordilleran Ice Sheet & Puget Sound Lobe Interactive | https://www.dnr.wa.gov/programs-and-services/geology/glaciers#the-cordilleran-ice-sheet.
  2. NOAA - Classifying Estuaries by Geology | https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_estuaries/est04_geology.html 
  3. Puget Sound as a Fjord Estuary | https://www.psp.wa.gov/NEP-puget-sound-estuary.php 
  4. National Wildlife Federation: Biodiversity in Puget Sound | https://www.nwf.org/Educational-Resources/Wildlife-Guide/Wild-Places/Puget-Sound 
  5. Puget Sound Partnership | https://www.psp.wa.gov/ 
  6. Friends of Waterfront Seattle | https://waterfrontseattle.org/ 
  7. UW Climate Science for the Classroom - Puget Sound Glacial History | https://uw.pressbooks.pub/climate/chapter/glacial-history-of-puget-sound-exploration/ 
  8. USGS - Groundwater Flooding in Glacial Terrain | https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2000/0111/report.pdf
  9. State of the Sound - https://stateofthesound.wa.gov/condition-of-the-puget-sound-ecosystem/

Disclaimers:
We acknowledge the following sources of analysis / information / images. All information was sourced using guidelines of "Fair Use," and all other information was "original work by students." No persons not a part of this team assisted with the project. All Geospatial Data was sourced from ArcGIS Online, using ESRI's Map Viewer Classic and ArcGIS Pro Desktop processes. Geospatial Data presented is overlayed layers on a basemap, and these layers rendered numeric data from the aforementioned sources.

results.title: WA State Cannabis Retailer Clusters and Median Household Income
results.description:
In November of 2012 Washington State passed Initiative 502, legalizing the sale, use and possession of recreational cannabis for adults. Starting in July of 2014, the State of Washington permitted the sale and distribution of recreational cannabis to customers aged 21+. This has brought a wide range of benefits ranging from the average individual looking for alternatives to alcohol or prescription medication, to state-wide tax revenue that brings in millions of dollars every year that are allocated to programs like public health, education, and drug rehabilitation (Santos 2021).

      Local/state government and city zoning play a large role in how cannabis retailers or distributed throughout a city. “[One] cannot set up a store within 1000 feet of any elementary or secondary school, playground, recreation center or facility, child care center, public park, public transit center, library, or game arcade that allows minors to enter.” (Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board).

      There are multiple purposes for this project; to update the state’s listing of cannabis retailers using ArcGIS, to identify clusters within specific communities, and to visually display surrounding income data of these retailers. Currently, the State of Washington does not have an updated spatial display of cannabis retailers. Due to cannabis retailers falling under specific guidelines, it’s a business that sells aged restricted products, and not to mention biases that individuals or communities have against the plant, there is a high possibility that clusters of retailers would occur.

      Upon gathering the addresses of cannabis retailers, I geocoded them into Arc in order to create a ‘CannabisRetailers’ point layer. This layer displays the real world addresses of Washington State cannabis retailers, in addition to other relevant information such as recent 2021 pre-tax sales of those shops.

      For the sake of this project, I analyzed all small cities in Washington of less than 40,000 with at least 3 cannabis retailers, in addition to all large cities in Washington over 80,000.

      Upon analyzing the small and large cities that I defined, there were some noticeable trends found in the data. The most common income tract for a cannabis retailer to be located are in neighborhoods with median household incomes between $35,000-$65,000, with 142 Washington cannabis retailers found in this category. The second most common income tract for cannabis retailers is the $65,000-$100,000 category, with 95 retailers found in that demographic. This trend can also be found when small and large cities’ data are observed separately. 

      Small and large cities exhibited a high likelihood of clusters of cannabis retailers as well. For the sake of this project, I define a ‘cluster’ as being the likelihood or probability of one exiting a cannabis shop and finding another cannabis shop 1 mile away or less away. 

Starting with large cities, 9/13 cities in this category had over a 50% likelihood for cannabis clusters. Seattle, Spokane and Bellingham have the highest probability of clusters occurring with percentages ranging between 75-83%.

A similar story can also be told about the smaller cities that I analyzed. Out of 22 small cities sampled in Washington State with at least 3 cannabis retailers, 20 of them had over a 50% likelihood for clusters occurring. This high probability was moderately expected with less land and overall space to be utilized in smaller communities.

Small and large cities in Washington also did not show a significant income range for their distribution of cannabis retailers. Only 3 cities had cannabis retailers stretch across four income demographic categories; Seattle, Spokane and Everett. It was very common to see a range of two to three income categories for any given city, but nothing over four. Granted, in order to have a fair range in this case, a prerequisite would be for a city to have a large diversity of income demographics to begin with.

      In conclusion, my spatial representation of cannabis retailers and income tract data has shown that cannabis retailers don’t have much room to work with, literally and figuratively speaking. Clusters are inevitable when it comes to retailer distribution; small cities have less land space to utilize which means less priority is given to cannabis retailers, and large cities are so densely populated that in order to be readily available to the consumer, more and more retailers are needed to incentivize competition within the industry. The demand is, and always was there among consumers from all walks of life, the supply, however, is distributed sporadically with the vast majority of retailers in Washington State being found in communities with median household incomes of $35,000-$65,000 per year.

results.title: Story Map
results.description:
This StoryMap examines the aspect of urban geography that most interested me this quarter: social areas of cities, particularly how neighbourhoods become segregated by race, income, and housing patterns. I feel like I learned a great deal from Map Exercise #6 about how cities are not random, but rather follow patterns such as the sector model, multiple nuclei model, and the concentric zone model. It was helpful to see real Census maps to understand how these patterns manifest in real cities today. For instance, Seattle's pattern of income and racial distribution clearly follows the "social areas" discussed in Chapter 11.

I liked this topic because it really showed how geography affects people's lives in ways that are not readily noticed. I found it interesting to see that house costs, transportation, school districts, zoning, and even past policies like redlining affect long-term trends in who has access to stable neighborhoods, good jobs, and education. That the subject was about actual maps made it more relatable to me, since I live in Washington, and the city discussed was Seattle. It shows that even in places that we consider to be "progressive," inequality can still be seen. It really helped me understand that it is not just physical space that geography represents, but power and social decisions.

results.title: ESRM 101 Tree Walk (University Heights neighborhood)
results.description: This tree walk occurs in the University Heights neighborhood (98105) in the University District (Unit 14). The area, which borders the residential and commercial zones, previously had one of Seattle's first public elementary schools, which operated from 1902 to 1989. The building and area were renovated and repurposed upon its closing into a community center and public park. In 2010, it was registered as a national heritage site by the US Interior Department because of its history, which is critical for conserving the surrounding ecosystem's integrity and biodiversity. This designation of status is beneficial for shaping the area's tree canopy today, as the area now has the government's resources to support the preservation of its landscape, allowing local trees in the area to receive the care they need. Because of the area's backstory and its designation of status, I felt that these policies allowed the best settings to create a tree walk.
results.snippet: This tree walk takes place in Unit 14: University District, located within a few minute's walk from the University of Washington.

results.title: ESRM 101: Tree Walk in Green Lake
results.description:
Introduction and Background

For this assignment, I went to the Green Lake Loop. According the Urban Tree Zone, it is defined as Unit #22 and has two zip codes which are 98103 and 98115. From the University of Washington campus, Green Lake is about a 10 minute drive away. I'm a local and have always known this place as somewhere people go for walks, biking, paddle-boarding and more recently-pickleball. I find this area super convenient for a large population of people because of its location in northern Seattle.

Green Lake is the remnant of Lake Russell which was created by glacier inflows. Since 1908 when the Board of Park Commissioners earned rights to the area that Green Lake is now, many amenities have been added. Aside from the staple, paved path that surrounds the actual lake itself, a formal playground, recreational water sport rentals, and pickleball-courts are also key components that add to the greater Green Lake community. The park is seen as a place where people can get out and active, often attracting dog owners, swimmers, runners, etc. Niche, a website that summarizes neighborhoods based on schools, safety, housing, etc., rates Green Lake as a comprehensive A+. This neighborhood is described as a mix between urban and suburban which adds to the attractiveness and versatility of this place- not just reside in, but to also hang out in.
